subject: Science
title: Year 9 Science Exam 1
intro: Calculator allowed. Relative atomic masses (A<sub>r</sub>): C = 12, O = 16, Fe = 56. For longer answers write in full sentences and use key words. Describe = say what happens; Explain = say what happens and why (use because and so); Compare = similarities and differences (use whereas); Evaluate = points for and against, then a justified conclusion. 6-mark questions are marked on how well your ideas link together: plan for a minute, then write about 6 linked points.

questions.q:
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an inherited disorder. It is caused by a recessive allele, f. The dominant allele is F.
What term describes different forms of the same gene?
questions.ms: allele (1).

questions.q:
Two parents do not have CF, but they are both carriers (genotype Ff).
Write out a genetic diagram (Punnett square) to show the possible genotypes of their children: give each parent's gametes and the four offspring genotypes. Identify the genotype of a child who would have CF.
questions.ms: Gametes F and f from each parent (1); offspring FF, Ff, Ff, ff (1); ff identified as the child with CF (1).

questions.q: Give the probability that a child of these parents will have CF.
questions.hint: Type it as a decimal, fraction or percentage, like 0.5 or 1/2 or 50%
questions.ms: 0.25 / 25% / 1 in 4 (1). Do not accept 1 : 4 or 1 : 3.

questions.q:
The couple's first child has CF. The parents say:
"Our first child has cystic fibrosis, so our next children will definitely not have it."
Evaluate this statement.
questions.ms: The statement is wrong (1); each pregnancy is independent, so every child has a 25% chance of CF (1).

questions.q:
Amira and Dana are identical twins. Amira is 8 kg heavier than Dana.
Explain why identical twins can have different body masses. Use ideas about genetic and environmental variation.
questions.ms: Any three: identical twins have the same genes / alleles / DNA (1); so the difference cannot be genetic (1); it is caused by the environment (1); e.g. different diet or amount of exercise (1).

questions.q:
MRSA is a strain of bacteria that is resistant to many antibiotics.
Explain how a population of antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA develops.
questions.ms: Four points in a logical order: a random mutation in the DNA of a bacterium (1); makes it resistant to the antibiotic (1); the antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria, resistant ones survive and reproduce (1); they pass on the resistance allele so the resistant population increases (1).

questions.q: Suggest two ways that doctors and patients can slow down the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
questions.ms: Any two: don't prescribe antibiotics for viral infections / unnecessarily (1); patients complete the full course (1); reduce antibiotic use in farming (1); better hospital hygiene (1).

questions.q:
The Arctic fox lives in the Arctic, where the ground is covered in snow for most of the year. It has thick white fur and small ears.
Explain how these adaptations of the Arctic fox developed by natural selection over many generations.
questions.ms: Level-marked. Level 3 (5–6): detailed and coherent, points linked in a logical sequence, correct terms. Level 2 (3–4): several relevant points with some linking. Level 1 (1–2): simple, separate statements. 0: nothing relevant. Indicative: variation in fur colour, thickness and ear size; caused by mutations / genetic; white fur camouflages in snow (catch prey, avoid predators); thick fur insulates; small ears reduce surface area and heat loss; these foxes more likely to survive; survivors reproduce and pass on alleles; over many generations the alleles become more common. Level 3 links a feature to a survival advantage AND to passing on alleles over generations.

questions.q:
A student wants to find out how the number of daisy plants changes with distance from a tall wall.
Describe a method the student could use to investigate this, using a transect and quadrats.
questions.ms: Level-marked. Level 3 (5–6): detailed and coherent, points linked in a logical sequence, correct terms. Level 2 (3–4): several relevant points with some linking. Level 1 (1–2): simple, separate statements. 0: nothing relevant. Indicative: tape measure in a straight line from the wall; quadrat at regular intervals (e.g. every 2 m); count daisies in each quadrat; rule for plants partly inside; repeat with more transects; mean for each distance; control variables (same quadrat size, same day/weather); measure light intensity with a light meter. Level 3: a clear method someone could follow, with repeats and a control variable.

questions.ms: 20 (Trial 3 at 4 m) (1).

questions.q: Calculate the mean number of daisies at 4 m. Do not include the anomalous result.
questions.ms: (7 + 6) ÷ 2 (1) = 6.5 (1). Correct answer alone scores 2.

questions.q: Describe the trend in the results and suggest an explanation. Use data from the table in your answer.
questions.ms: As distance increases the number of daisies increases from 1 to 12, levelling off after 8 m (1). Near the wall there is more shade / less light for photosynthesis (1).

questions.q:
In a blast furnace, iron oxide reacts with carbon monoxide to produce iron and carbon dioxide.
Balance the equation: Fe₂O₃ + ___ CO → ___ Fe + ___ CO₂
questions.hint: Type the three missing numbers in order, like 1,2,3
questions.ms: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (1).

questions.q: Calculate the relative formula mass (M<sub>r</sub>) of iron oxide, Fe₂O₃.
Calculate the maximum mass of iron that can be produced from 320 g of iron oxide. (g)
questions.ms: 224 g. 160 g of Fe₂O₃ gives 2 × 56 = 112 g Fe (1); 320 g is 2 × 160 g (1); 2 × 112 = 224 g (1). Allow the mole method. Correct answer alone scores 3.

questions.q: In a test run, only 190 g of iron was collected. Calculate the percentage yield. Give your answer to 2 significant figures. (%)
Give two reasons why the actual yield of a reaction is often lower than the theoretical yield.
questions.ms: Any two: reaction may not go to completion (1); product lost when separated (1); side reactions (1); impure reactant (1).

questions.q: Which metal must be extracted from its ore by electrolysis?
questions.ms: aluminium (1).

questions.q:
Electrolysis is more expensive than extracting a metal by heating its oxide with carbon.
Explain why electrolysis is expensive and why it must still be used for some metals.
questions.ms: Uses large amounts of electricity / energy (1); the ore must be melted, needing high temperatures (1); used for metals more reactive than carbon, because carbon cannot reduce them / remove the oxygen (1).

questions.q:
Petrol and diesel cars release harmful gases such as carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides. Most cars are fitted with a catalytic converter.
Explain how a catalytic converter reduces the harm caused by exhaust gases. Then evaluate whether catalytic converters solve the problem of pollution from cars.
questions.ms: Level-marked. Level 3 (5–6): detailed and coherent, points linked in a logical sequence, correct terms. Level 2 (3–4): several relevant points with some linking. Level 1 (1–2): simple, separate statements. 0: nothing relevant. How it works: platinum / rhodium catalysts; honeycomb gives large surface area so faster reactions; CO + O₂ → CO₂ (CO is toxic); nitrogen oxides → nitrogen + oxygen (acid rain, breathing problems); catalyst not used up. Evaluation: reduces CO and NOx; but still makes CO₂ (greenhouse gas); only works when hot (short journeys); doesn't remove particulates; platinum expensive and rare; conclusion: reduces some pollution but doesn't solve it. No evaluation caps at Level 2.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of continuous variation?
questions.ms: height (1).

questions.q: Which of these is an abiotic factor?
questions.ms: soil pH (1).

questions.q: Compare sexual reproduction with asexual reproduction.
questions.ms: Any four; full marks need a similarity or comparative words (whereas): two parents vs one (1); gametes / fertilisation vs none (1); variation vs identical clones (1); asexual faster / less energy, no mate needed (1); similarity: both produce offspring / pass on genetic information (1).

questions.q: Some plant species are in danger of becoming extinct. Explain how a gene bank (seed bank) can help prevent this.
questions.ms: Seeds / genetic material stored safely, e.g. frozen (1); so plants can be regrown if the species dies out in the wild (1).
